We introduce an operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses: evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties, coupled with feasible investigations, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations. Our DiscoveryRSI framework develops hypothesis trees through multi-agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and recursively learns through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization attributes scientific assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay identifies productive strategies and recurring failures to refine research workflows; and rediscovery applies accepted improvements to new investigations, generating further experience for subsequent learning. We also introduce DFM-Bench, which provides comprehensive assessment of hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress at the levels of hypotheses, revisions, development paths and research runs. Across four life-science domains, automated evaluation shows that hypothesis quality rises from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self-improvement, with the large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability. We further validate hypothesis quality through expert review, comparing our DiscoveryRSI-27B with other research agents. Preliminary human assessments show that DiscoveryRSI-27B scores higher than GPT-6 Luna on hypothesis importance and whether claims are plausible and evidence-bounded. DiscoveryRSI-27B achieved a 6.3% rate of hypothesis correspondence with research published after the model cutoff, largely outperform GPT-6 with 2.5% and Claude Opus 5 with 2.3%, while delivering greater human-rated improvement along research paths.

frontier.title: Self-Building Labs
frontier.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for. Adapting them to a new experiment still requires extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setup given a high-level scientific goal. SBL starts from whatever already exists, from an empty room to a working SDL, and builds the missing capabilities: the lab layout, its digital twin, robot skills, and experimental workflows. We demonstrate the system working across different robots and setups, scaling from a single workstation to laboratories with several robots working together. We validate SBL's end-to-end capabilities through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment. By shifting human researchers from manually configuring and programming device automation to specifying scientific objectives, SBL makes scientific automation more accessible, flexible, and scalable. Project website: https://self-building-labs.github.io/

frontier.title: Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models
frontier.abstract: Video generative models are an emerging tool for embodied agents: they can serve as scalable visual planners, generating videos that depict how to complete previously unseen tasks. However, executing these plans typically requires a video-to-action or "inverse dynamics" model trained on large, human-collected video-action datasets, severely limiting scalability. We introduce Mirror, a self-supervised approach that learns video-to-action mappings through environment interactions, without prior action data or hand-crafted rewards. Mirror learns by attempting to follow a visual plan by executing its best guess of the underlying actions in the environment. Mirror then trains on the resulting video-action pairs, incrementally self-improving and following the visual planner more closely. Across Atari, OGBench, and DeepMind Control, Mirror outperforms leading learning-from-observation methods with learned video plans, and achieves near-expert performance with oracle plans. On Minecraft BASALT, it outperforms methods with access to expert actions or hand-engineered task knowledge. In Minecraft survival, it is the first method to acquire an iron pickaxe through self-improvement alone, without rewards or expert action labels. In the offline setting, with expert action labels but no environment interaction, it sets a new state of the art in obtaining diamonds. Our results suggest that advances in video models can translate into increasingly capable agents without a corresponding need for hand-crafted rewards or large collections of expert action data.

frontier.title: Advancing Large Language Model Attribution through Self-Improving
frontier.abstract: Teaching large language models (LLMs) to generate text with citations to evidence sources can mitigate hallucinations and enhance verifiability in information-seeking systems. However, improving this capability requires high-quality attribution data, which is costly and labor-intensive. Inspired by recent advances in self-improvement that enhance LLMs without manual annotation, we present START, a Self-Taught AttRibuTion framework for iteratively improving the attribution capability of LLMs. First, to prevent models from stagnating due to initially insufficient supervision signals, START leverages the model to self-construct synthetic training data for warming up. To further self-improve the model’s attribution ability, START iteratively utilizes fine-grained preference supervision signals constructed from its sampled responses to encourage robust, comprehensive, and attributable generation. Experiments on three open-domain question-answering datasets, covering long-form QA and multi-step reasoning, demonstrate significant performance gains of 25.13% on average without relying on human annotations and more advanced models. Further analysis reveals that START excels in aggregating information across multiple sources.

frontier.title: BC-Prover: Backward Chaining Prover for Formal Theorem Proving
frontier.abstract: Despite the remarkable progress made by large language models in mathematical reasoning, interactive theorem proving in formal logic still remains a prominent challenge. Previous methods resort to neural models for proofstep generation and search. However, they suffer from exploring possible proofsteps empirically in a large search space. Moreover, they directly use a less rigorous informal proof for proofstep generation, neglecting the incomplete reasoning within. In this paper, we propose BC-Prover, a backward chaining framework guided by pseudo steps. Specifically, BC-Prover prioritizes pseudo steps to proofstep generation. The pseudo steps boost the proof construction in two aspects: (1) Backward Chaining that decomposes the proof into sub-goals for goal-oriented exploration. (2) Step Planning that makes a fine-grained planning to bridge the gap between informal and formal proofs. Experiments on the miniF2F benchmark show significant performance gains by our framework over the state-of-the-art approaches. Our framework is also compatible with existing provers and further improves their performance with the backward chaining technique.

frontier.title: BitDistiller: Unleashing the Potential of Sub-4-Bit LLMs via Self-Distillation
frontier.abstract: The upscaling of Large Language Models (LLMs) has yielded impressive advances in natural language processing, yet it also poses significant deployment challenges. Weight quantization has emerged as a widely embraced solution to reduce memory and computational demands. This paper introduces BitDistiller, a framework that synergizes Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) with Knowledge Distillation (KD) to boost the performance of LLMs at ultra-low precisions (sub-4-bit). Specifically, BitDistiller first incorporates a tailored asymmetric quantization and clipping technique to maximally preserve the fidelity of quantized weights, and then proposes a novel Confidence-Aware Kullback-Leibler Divergence (CAKLD) objective, which is employed in a self-distillation manner to enable faster convergence and superior model performance. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that BitDistiller significantly surpasses existing methods in both 3-bit and 2-bit configurations on general language understanding and complex reasoning benchmarks. Notably, BitDistiller is shown to be more cost-effective, demanding fewer data and training resources. The code is available at

frontier.title: Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
frontier.abstract: In the age of mobile internet, user data, often referred to as memories, is continuously generated on personal devices. Effectively managing and utilizing this data to deliver services to users is a compelling research topic. In this paper, we introduce a novel task of crafting personalized agents powered by large language models (LLMs), which utilize a user’s smartphone memories to enhance downstream applications with advanced LLM capabilities. To achieve this goal, we introduce EMG-RAG, a solution that combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) techniques with an Editable Memory Graph (EMG). This approach is further optimized using Reinforcement Learning to address three distinct challenges: data collection, editability, and selectability. Extensive experiments on a real-world dataset validate the effectiveness of EMG-RAG, achieving an improvement of approximately 10% over the best existing approach. Additionally, the personalized agents have been transferred into a real smartphone AI assistant, which leads to enhanced usability.

frontier.title: Disentangling Memory and Reasoning Ability in Large Language Models
frontier.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in handling complex tasks that require both extensive knowledge and reasoning abilities. However, the existing LLM inference pipeline operates as an opaque process without explicit separation between knowledge retrieval and reasoning steps, making the model’s decision-making process unclear and disorganized. Recent research has shown that this ambiguity will lead to issues such as knowledge forgetting, which significantly impact the reliability of LLMs. In this paper, we propose a novel language model inference paradigm that decomposes the complex inference process into two distinct and clear actions:

frontier.title: EscapeBench: Towards Advancing Creative Intelligence of Language Model Agents
frontier.abstract: Language model agents excel in long-session planning and reasoning, but existing benchmarks primarily focus on goal-oriented tasks with explicit objectives, neglecting creative adaptation in unfamiliar environments. To address this, we introduce EscapeBench—a benchmark suite of room escape game environments designed to challenge agents with creative reasoning, unconventional tool use, and iterative problem-solving to uncover implicit goals. Our results show that current LM models, despite employing working memory and Chain-of-Thought reasoning, achieve only 15% average progress without hints, highlighting their limitations in creativity. To bridge this gap, we propose EscapeAgent, a framework designed to enhance creative reasoning through Foresight (innovative tool use) and Reflection (identifying unsolved tasks). Experiments show that EscapeAgent can execute action chains over 1,000 steps while maintaining logical coherence. It navigates and completes games with up to 40% fewer steps and hints, performs robustly across difficulty levels, and achieves higher action success rates with more efficient and innovative puzzle-solving strategies.

frontier.title: In-the-wild Audio Spatialization with Flexible Text-guided Localization
frontier.abstract: Binaural audio enriches immersive experiences by enabling the perception of the spatial locations of sounding objects in AR, VR, and embodied AI applications. While existing audio spatialization methods can generally map any available monaural audio to binaural audio signals, they often lack the flexible and interactive control needed in complex multi-object user-interactive environments. To address this, we propose a Text-guided Audio Spatialization (TAS) framework that utilizes diverse text prompts and evaluates our model from unified generation and comprehension perspectives. Due to the limited availability of high-quality, large-scale stereo data, we construct the SpatialTAS dataset, which encompasses 376,000 simulated binaural audio samples to facilitate the training of our model. Our model learns binaural differences guided by 3D spatial location and relative position prompts, enhanced with flipped-channel audio. Experimental results show that our model can generate high quality binaural audios for various audio types on both simulated and real-recorded datasets. Besides, we establish an assessment model based on Llama-3.1-8B, which evaluates the semantic accuracy of spatial locations through a spatial reasoning task. Results demonstrate that by utilizing text prompts for flexible and interactive control, we can generate binaural audio with both high quality and semantic consistency in spatial locations.

frontier.title: Learning Global Controller in Latent Space for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
frontier.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have showcased remarkable prowess in various natural language processing tasks, their training costs are exorbitant. Consequently, a plethora of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods have emerged to tailor large models for downstream tasks, including low-rank training. Recent approaches either amalgamate existing fine-tuning methods or dynamically adjust rank allocation. Nonetheless, these methods continue to grapple with issues like local optimization, inability to train with full rank and lack of focus on specific tasks. In this paper, we introduce an innovative parameter-efficient method for exploring optimal solutions within latent space. More specifically, we introduce a set of latent units designed to iteratively extract input representations from LLMs, continuously refining informative features that enhance downstream task performance. Due to the small and independent nature of the latent units in relation to input size, this significantly reduces training memory requirements. Additionally, we employ an asymmetric attention mechanism to facilitate bidirectional interaction between latent units and freezed LLM representations, thereby mitigating issues associated with non-full-rank training. Furthermore, we apply distillation over hidden states during the interaction, which guarantees a trimmed number of trainable parameters.Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on a range of natural language understanding, generation and reasoning tasks.

frontier.title: Learning Planning-based Reasoning by Trajectories Collection and Process Reward Synthesizing
frontier.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant potential in handling complex reasoning tasks through step-by-step rationale generation. However, recent studies have raised concerns regarding the hallucination and flaws in their reasoning process. Substantial efforts are being made to improve the reliability and faithfulness of the generated rationales. Some approaches model reasoning as planning, while others focus on annotating for process supervision. Nevertheless, the planning-based search process often results in high latency due to the frequent assessment of intermediate reasoning states and the extensive exploration space. Additionally, supervising the reasoning process with human annotation is costly and challenging to scale for LLM training. To address these issues, in this paper, we propose a framework to learn planning-based reasoning through Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) on collected trajectories, which are ranked according to synthesized process rewards. Our results on challenging logical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our learning framework, showing that our 7B model can surpass the strong counterparts like GPT-3.5-Turbo.

frontier.title: Open Grounded Planning: Challenges and Benchmark Construction
frontier.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has increasingly drawn attention to the use of LLMs for human-like planning. Existing work on LLM-based planning either focuses on leveraging the inherent language generation capabilities of LLMs to produce free-style plans, or employs reinforcement learning approaches to learn decision-making for a limited set of actions within restricted environments. However, both approaches exhibit significant discrepancies from the open and executable requirements in real-world planning. In this paper, we propose a new planning task–open grounded planning. The primary objective of open grounded planning is to ask the model to generate an executable plan based on a variable action set, thereby ensuring the executability of the produced plan. To this end, we establishes a benchmark for open grounded planning spanning a wide range of domains. Then we test current state-of-the-art LLMs along with five planning approaches, revealing that existing LLMs and methods still struggle to address the challenges posed by grounded planning in open domains. The outcomes of this paper define and establish a foundational dataset for open grounded planning, and shed light on the potential challenges and future directions of LLM-based planning.

frontier.title: Persuading across Diverse Domains: a Dataset and Persuasion Large Language Model
frontier.abstract: Persuasive dialogue requires multi-turn following and planning abilities to achieve the goal of persuading users, which is still challenging even for state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs). Previous works focus on retrieval-based models or generative models in a specific domain due to a lack of data across multiple domains. In this paper, we leverage GPT-4 to create the first multi-domain persuasive dialogue dataset DailyPersuasion. Then we propose a general method named PersuGPT to learn a persuasion model based on LLMs through intent-to-strategy reasoning, which summarizes the intent of user’s utterance and reasons next strategy to respond. Moreover, we design a simulation-based preference optimization, which utilizes a learned user model and our model to simulate next turns and estimate their rewards more accurately. Experimental results on two datasets indicate that our proposed method outperforms all baselines in terms of automatic evaluation metric Win-Rate and human evaluation. The code and data are available at

frontier.title: Planning Like Human: A Dual-process Framework for Dialogue Planning
frontier.abstract: In proactive dialogue, the challenge lies not just in generating responses but in steering conversations toward predetermined goals, a task where Large Language Models (LLMs) typically struggle due to their reactive nature. Traditional approaches to enhance dialogue planning in LLMs, ranging from elaborate prompt engineering to the integration of policy networks, either face efficiency issues or deliver suboptimal performance. Inspired by the dual-process theory in psychology, which identifies two distinct modes of thinking—intuitive (fast) and analytical (slow), we propose the Dual-Process Dialogue Planning (DPDP) framework. DPDP embodies this theory through two complementary planning systems: an instinctive policy model for familiar contexts and a deliberative Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) mechanism for complex, novel scenarios. This dual strategy is further coupled with a novel two-stage training regimen: offline Reinforcement Learning for robust initial policy model formation followed by MCTS-enhanced on-the-fly learning, which ensures a dynamic balance between efficiency and strategic depth. Our empirical evaluations across diverse dialogue tasks affirm DPDP’s superiority in achieving both high-quality dialogues and operational efficiency, outpacing existing methods.

frontier.title: SportsMetrics: Blending Text and Numerical Data to Understand Information Fusion in LLMs
frontier.abstract: Large language models hold significant potential for integrating various data types, such as text documents and database records, for advanced analytics. However, blending text and numerical data presents substantial challenges. LLMs need to process and cross-reference entities and numbers, handle data inconsistencies and redundancies, and develop planning capabilities such as building a working memory for managing complex data queries. In this paper, we introduce four novel tasks centered around sports data analytics to evaluate the numerical reasoning and information fusion capabilities of LLMs. These tasks involve providing LLMs with detailed, play-by-play sports game descriptions, then challenging them with adversarial scenarios such as new game rules, longer durations, scrambled narratives, and analyzing key statistics in game summaries. We conduct extensive experiments on NBA and NFL games to assess the performance of LLMs on these tasks. Our benchmark, SportsMetrics, introduces a new mechanism for assessing LLMs’ numerical reasoning and fusion skills.

frontier.title: ToolHop: A Query-Driven Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Multi-Hop Tool Use
frontier.abstract: Effective evaluation of multi-hop tool use is critical for analyzing the understanding, reasoning, and function-calling capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, progress has been hindered by a lack of reliable evaluation datasets. To address this, we present ToolHop, a dataset comprising 995 user queries and 3,912 associated tools, specifically designed for rigorous evaluation of multi-hop tool use. ToolHop ensures diverse queries, meaningful interdependencies, locally executable tools, detailed feedback, and verifiable answers through a novel query-driven data construction approach that includes tool creation, document refinement, and code generation. We evaluate 14 LLMs across five model families (i.e., LLaMA3.1, Qwen2.5, Gemini1.5, Claude3.5, and GPT), uncovering significant challenges in handling multi-hop tool-use scenarios. The leading model, GPT-4o, achieves an accuracy of 49.04%, underscoring substantial room for improvement. Further analysis reveals variations in tool-use strategies for various families, offering actionable insights to guide the development of more effective approaches. Code and data can be found in

frontier.title: VisualWebArena: Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Realistic Visual Web Tasks
frontier.abstract: Autonomous agents capable of planning, reasoning, and executing actions on the web offer a promising avenue for automating computer tasks. However, the majority of existing benchmarks primarily focus on text-based agents, neglecting many natural tasks that require visual information to effectively solve. Given that most computer interfaces cater to human perception, visual information often augments textual data in ways that text-only models struggle to harness effectively. To bridge this gap, we introduce VisualWebArena, a benchmark designed to assess the performance of multimodal web agents on

frontier.title: Build, Don't Play: Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players
frontier.abstract: Can LLM agents carry a hard real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against people? We study this in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, an eight-player auto-battler with stochastic shops and battles, hidden information and nearly a thousand interacting cards. We present AutoTavern, a self-improving research system: specialised LLM research agents share a typed research memory, every claim passes verification gates, and live games close the loop, so the agents improve the simulator, opponents and policy and, from the same feedback, their own research process; a human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. In 20 days AutoTavern built TavernGym, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game, and delivered 23 versions of TavernAgent, trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real games. TavernAgent plays complete games on the live ladder by itself: its rating rose from 6,000 to about 15,000 and, on the public leaderboard's measure, its last 20 records average a placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, better than the server's ten highest-rated players on every statistic (2.34, 59%). TavernBench, 960 tasks in 40 scenarios, shows that the system the agents built is the strongest player: TavernAgent answers 91% of the play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in 0.03 s where they need up to 26 s; within the second a live turn allows, it keeps 90% and no LLM more than 26%. LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TavernBench and TavernGym at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern.

frontier.title: Microscopic robots that sense, think, act, and compute
frontier.abstract: Although miniaturization has been a goal in robotics for nearly 40 years, roboticists have struggled to access submillimeter dimensions without making sacrifices to onboard information processing because of the unique physics of the microscale. Consequently, microrobots often lack the key features that distinguish their macroscopic cousins from other machines, namely, on-robot systems for decision-making, sensing, feedback, and programmable computation. Here, we take up the challenge of building a robot comparable in size to a single-celled paramecium that can sense, think, and act using onboard systems for computation, sensing, memory, locomotion, and communication. Built massively in parallel with fully lithographic processing, these microrobots can execute digitally defined algorithms and autonomously change behavior in response to their surroundings. Combined, these results pave the way for general-purpose microrobots that can be programmed many times in a simple setup and can work together to carry out tasks without supervision in uncertain environments.

frontier.title: Whole-Body Integrated Motion Planning for Aerial Manipulators
DREAM: Decentralized Real-Time Asynchronous Probabilistic Trajectory Planning for Collision-Free Multirobot Navigation in Cluttered Environments
Duo: A Reciprocal World Model for Full-Duplex Interaction
frontier.abstract: In this report, we introduce the Reciprocal World Model (RWM) and present Duo v1, a full-duplex world model that continuously perceives audiovisual inputs while responding to users in real time. The RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental to what constitutes a world. Existing world models largely focus on simulating the latter, leaving reasoning and decision-making as external controls rather than intrinsic parts of the world itself. In RWM, we identify two equally fundamental capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audio-visual behavior. To realize this formulation, Duo v1 introduces three key technical designs: (1) Leveraging autoregressive modeling for continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions, rather than restricting it to instruction understanding for diffusion models. (2) Constructing chunk-specific conditions and synchronize tokens across Intent and Realization on a unified timeline. Module-specific attention masks enforce causal dependencies both within and across chunks, preventing access to future inputs. (3) Mitigating distribution shift in both modules through dual rollout distillation, training on autoregressively generated Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories from Realization. Both modules continuously perceive real-time audio, video, and text, enabling full-duplex interaction with spontaneous conversations and interruptions. Beyond conversation, users can share real objects, reshape virtual scenes, guide assistants, or play audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls. The release of Duo v1 makes our first step, with the next version coming soon. We look forward to broader exploration of this emerging field.

frontier.title: Memory-Centric Continual Learning for AI Agents
frontier.abstract: Autonomous agents powered by foundation models can reason, plan, and use tools, but their fixed weights and context limits hinder sustained learning from experience over long-term deployment. While external memory systems attempt to bridge this gap, they mostly act as passive retrieval caches, evaluated primarily by whether they can recall stored facts or past interactions. Whether memory can drive genuine continual learning remains an open question. In this paper, we introduce Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL), arguing that memory should be judged by whether it improves future actions, not merely what it retrieves. MCCL has three main parts. First, a three-axis taxonomy organizes memory by where state is stored (substrates), what form it takes (assets), and how it is managed (policies). This defines a two-loop lifecycle that updates memory state in an inner loop while refining management policies in an outer loop based on task feedback. Second, an evaluation protocol measures retention under interference, adaptation to change, and task transfer to isolate genuine behavioral gains from simple context expansion. Third, a memory scaling framework models how agent performance scales with experience, storage capacity, and compute budgets across non-parametric and parametric memory. Together, these components reframe agent memory from passive lookup to continuous learning, offering a principled route toward self-improving autonomous agents.

frontier.title: Medical needles in the hands of AI: Advancing toward autonomous robotic navigation
frontier.abstract: Safely and accurately navigating needles percutaneously or endoscopically to sites deep within the body is essential for many medical procedures, from biopsies to localized drug deliveries to tumor ablations. The advent of image guidance decades ago gave physicians information about the patient’s anatomy. We are now entering the era of AI (artificial intelligence) guidance, where AI can automatically analyze images, identify targets and obstacles, compute safe trajectories, and autonomously navigate a needle to a site with unprecedented accuracy and precision. We survey recent advances in the building blocks of AI guidance for medical needle deployment robots (perceiving anatomy, planning motions, perceiving instrument state, and performing motions) and discuss research opportunities to maximize the benefits of AI guidance for patient care.

frontier.title: Sequential memory improves sample and memory efficiency in episodic control
AWAM: Active Trajectory-Conditioned View Imagination for Robust Robot Manipulation
frontier.abstract: Rapid progress in embodied intelligence has enabled increasingly capable robots to follow language instructions and manipulate diverse objects. However, strong results in structured environments do not automatically transfer to open-world conditions, where clutter, occlusion, and changing viewpoints can obscure the spatial relationships required for action. To address this perceptual gap, a virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced. AWAM, an Active World-Action Model actively plans where to observe and imagines what will be seen along the planned trajectory before acting. Task-related virtual camera motion is predicted and used as a structured query into a geometry-conditioned world model, producing a reusable spatial prior for manipulation, which is later compressed into a fixed memory and fused with live observations through cross-attention for diffusion-based action prediction. AWAM achieves competitive success rates with 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials. These results support improved robustness to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts, addressing part of the gap between structured manipulation and less controlled environments.

frontier.title: Beckmann World Models: Direct Terminal-Map Learning for One-Step Action-Conditioned Prediction
frontier.abstract: Action-conditioned world models support planning and policy evaluation by predicting future states. However, learning an accurate one-step predictor can require substantial training computation. We introduce Beckmann World Models (BWM), which learn a direct map from noise, visual history, and actions to future frames without a pretrained generative teacher. We adapt the terminal-map conservation law of Beckmann Transport Models to action-conditioned video prediction, training directly from noise-data pairs without conditional populations of generated samples required by DriftWorld. However, transport consistency on interpolated inputs does not ensure accurate prediction from the pure noise used at inference. We address this gap with endpoint-aligned training that directly supervises the source prediction, emphasizes motion and spatial structure, and teaches recovery from generated histories. All components train the same map and retain one network call per future chunk. On PushT and Robomimic Can, the final model reduces 64-frame prediction MSE by 68% and 57%, respectively, relative to same-backbone regression baseline. For policy evaluation, BWM achieves the lowest mean IoU error among the evaluated models, 0.0100, at 24.8 ms per four-frame PushT prediction. On Robomimic Can, the BWM stage trained with motion supervision and generated histories achieves 3.3 times higher throughput and 78% lower peak memory than local one-step DriftWorld. In a latent-space extension to RT-1 and Bridge-V2, equal-update controls show that feature supervision under generated histories improves perceptual prediction. These findings show how terminal-map learning can combine efficient training with accurate one-step visual prediction.

frontier.title: Beyond Action Prediction: Learning Search-Free Planning in Latent Space
frontier.abstract: Latent world models learn action-conditioned state transitions in a compact representation space, providing a predictive model for visual planning and control. However, planning with these models typically requires costly test-time optimization over action sequences. We propose to replace this online search with a goal-conditioned inverse model that directly predicts actions from current and goal observations. A key challenge is that action prediction alone neither ensures that goal representations encode action-relevant information nor that predicted actions are consistent with the learned latent prediction model. We introduce Hindsight Inverse JEPA Planning (HIJP), a search-free framework that addresses both aspects during training. HIJP relabels future observations along offline trajectories as goals, providing action supervision across multiple temporal horizons. By retaining gradients through the goal representations, this supervision directly shapes the visual representation. HIJP further feeds predicted actions into the latent predictor model and aligns the resulting next-state representations with encoded successor observations, enforcing action-transition consistency. At inference time, the inverse dynamics model and latent predictor models are applied alternately to generate multi-step action sequences without online search. Across four visual control tasks, HIJP achieves 86.8% overall success and a 1.9-16.5x planning speedup over search-based planning.

frontier.title: Beyond Success Rate: Interventional Evaluation of Memory in Vision-Language-Action Systems
frontier.abstract: When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role? Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide offsetting gains and losses. We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) for vision-language-action (VLA) systems to address four questions: (1) Does memory provide a net benefit? (2) Under what conditions does memory help? (3) Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? (4) Are these effects specific to task-relevant facts? At the retrieval interface, we compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect over fact-preserving replacements. To examine when memory helps, we introduce ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in current observations. The full memory configuration raises task success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under shared recorded executions. These results show that correct history can support robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.

frontier.title: Execution Before Memory: Diagnosing Memory Failures in Video World Models
frontier.abstract: A memory test for a video world model should say whether the scene was set, whether the asked change was carried out, and whether the last frame shows the result. Current tests fold these into one number, so a low score is easy to read as forgetting. When the change is not carried out, the hidden state transition cannot appear, so the test is not really a test of memory. We introduce MIST, an evaluation that separates the change from the memory it should leave behind. The model first sets the scene while the change stays hidden, and only later is asked to show it, with leakage before that point kept under control. This separation locates the bottleneck: the model sets the scene but does not carry out the instructed change. The same gap appears in general memory evaluations. On that basis we propose M3-Agent (Make the Missing Move), which recursively revises the details of the input instruction so that the model successfully carries out the requested instruction. Relative to the baseline, it more than triples the MIST reveal score. On the benchmarks, WRBench's score T rises by 26.1% and MBench-T's score U by 52.7%. The method meets the problem from the execution side: it shows what the frozen model can do once the move is stated, and it sets a stricter baseline.

frontier.title: Persistent Planar Memory for Video World Models
frontier.abstract: Video world models that generate and explore environments at scale need a persistent 3D memory of what they have produced. Plane primitives offer a natural candidate: a compact set of oriented planes captures the dominant structural elements (e.g., walls, floors, facades) of indoor and outdoor scenes, while requiring only 7 parameters per primitive. We present PPMem, a video world model that adopts plane primitives as its persistent 3D memory. PPMem augments a video diffusion transformer with a planar prediction head and a Depth Token Fusion (DTF) module: each autoregressive chunk jointly produces RGB video and planar geometry, which merges into a persistent plane memory that conditions subsequent chunks via rendered depth. The resulting memory is three orders of magnitude more compact than per-pixel point clouds (~100K primitives, 5MB for a full scene), geometrically explicit (metric depth, normals, exportable surfaces), cross-view consistent (jointly predicted by the shared backbone), and adaptive (refined by the merging procedure as generation proceeds). On DL3DV and RealEstate10K, PPMem outperforms prior 3D-grounded world models in video quality while jointly producing metric-scale depth, surface normals, and exportable planar geometry, sustaining coherence across hundreds of frames under large viewpoint changes. Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/ppmem.

frontier.title: GenTranslate: Large Language Models are Generative Multilingual Speech and Machine Translators
frontier.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have stepped forward the development of multilingual speech and machine translation by its reduced representation errors and incorporated external knowledge. However, both translation tasks typically utilize beam search decoding and top-1 hypothesis selection for inference. These techniques struggle to fully exploit the rich information in the diverse N-best hypotheses, making them less optimal for translation tasks that require a single, high-quality output sequence. In this paper, we propose a new generative paradigm for translation tasks, namely GenTranslate, which builds upon LLMs to generate better results from the diverse translation versions in N-best list. Leveraging the rich linguistic knowledge and strong reasoning abilities of LLMs, our new paradigm can integrate the diverse N-best candidates to generate a higher-quality translation result. Furthermore, to support LLM finetuning, we build and release a HypoTranslate dataset that contains over 592K hypotheses-translation pairs in 11 languages. Experiments on various speech and machine translation benchmarks (e.g., FLEURS, CoVoST-2, WMT) demonstrate that our GenTranslate significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art model.

frontier.title: The Mars 2020 OnBoard Planner: Increasing autonomy mission productivity of the Perseverance rover
frontier.abstract: Operators of planetary rovers, under strict energy and thermal constraints, face substantial challenges in maintaining high levels of rover productivity because of conservative ground-based planning and long communication latencies. In October 2023, to overcome these limits and increase science return, the Mars 2020 mission deployed OnBoard Planner into Perseverance rover operations. OnBoard Planner uses artificial intelligence constraint–based search to dynamically construct and modify activity schedules on board, adapting to real-time changes in rover state and martian environmental conditions. By replacing conservative ground predictions with real-time resource tracking, the system dynamically adjusts heating durations, reclaims unused schedule margin, and inserts opportunistic activities when extra resources become available. Here, we report on OnBoard Planner’s performance on Mars across more than 2 years of surface operations. The results demonstrate that OnBoard Planner increased discretionary rover activity by 10.5% overall while also improving the thermal and temporal conditions for certain types of scientific observations. Furthermore, the system achieved these productivity gains without increasing ground operations timelines. These findings are part of why OnBoard Planner has successfully become a standard part of Mars 2020 operations and demonstrate how dynamic onboard autonomy can enable resource-efficient operations for complex robotic systems in deep-space environments.

frontier.title: C$^{*}$: A Coverage Path Planning Algorithm for Unknown Environments Using Rapidly Covering Graphs
Adversarially Attacking Symbolic Vocabulary Vulnerabilities In LLM Planners
frontier.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, their abilities in navigating automated planning tasks have become essential. However, despite their strengths, LLMs' planning ability is not robust, particularly when they are not allowed to exploit commonsense cues in the symbolic vocabulary (e.g., names of actions, predicates, and objects) used to define planning tasks. This makes LLMs unreliable compared to symbolic planners. With recent reasoning models showing improved planning performance on tasks with obfuscated symbolic vocabularies, we utilize an adversarial attack framework to reveal to what extent the crucial weaknesses of LLM agents at joint symbolic interpretation and planning remain and whether they can reason properly when presented with severe cases. As such, our main contribution is devising an LLM-based attack model, which we call Symbolic Swapper, to automatically generate obfuscated planning domains with non-standard symbolic vocabularies that systematically break strong reasoning models' ability to plan. In doing so, we reveal how much LLMs' planning abilities can be further degraded under more advanced obfuscation schemes, allowing us to ascertain their success when having to rely on their pure planning ability. We find that attacks can decrease the planning performance of base models and even robust planning frameworks by over 70%. We further analyze the factors behind how LLM planning abilities break down and find that successful obfuscation causes models to appear to significantly degrade in reasoning quality despite them showing some inherent ability to understand the domain, revealing a gap in the perception of a task domain and being able to plan under it.

frontier.title: Agent-as-a-Judge
frontier.abstract: Artificial intelligence has progressed from task-specific systems toward general models spanning perception, generation, reasoning, and autonomous interaction, making reliable evaluation essential for comparison, deployment, and post-training feedback. At scale, modern evaluation pipelines increasingly rely on LLM-as-a-Judge to produce scores, preferences, and critiques; in its fixed-context setting, the judge relies on the supplied evaluand and evaluation materials. Yet a reliable verdict may require evidence beyond the supplied evaluand and context---either because critical environmental states remain unrecorded in the static execution log, or because controversial factual claims require external verification. Passive judges cannot obtain that missing evidence before deciding, especially when evaluating agent trajectories, executable artifacts, or domain-specific reports. Recent work therefore develops active evaluators that seek missing evidence and update their grounds for judgment before deciding. We bring these advances together through Agent-as-a-Judge, focusing on how evaluators construct and control checking processes within the broader LLM-based judging landscape. We define the scope through evaluation-directed checks and the use of their results, covering both structured workflows and observation-driven control. We organize the design space by multi-agent collaboration, tool integration, memory, and planning, and show how these mechanisms supply the checks and evidence on which a verdict rests. We consolidate published scores and reproduce missing entries for key agentic judges; the comparison reveals uneven agentic gains and motivates dedicated agentic evaluation. We conclude by characterizing application demands and open challenges in cost, reliability, safety, and governance that condition trusted deployment of agentic judges at scale.

frontier.title: Direction or Magnitude? Learning Scalars over Task-Calibrated Directions
frontier.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR, which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. The combination of adaptation quality, a compact trainable state, and training efficiency makes SCALAR a promising approach to resource-constrained fine-tuning.

frontier.title: ESI: An Embodied Self-Improvement Flywheel for LLM-VLA Agents
frontier.abstract: Independently pretrained language models and vision-language-action (VLA) policies provide complementary building blocks for embodied agents, but connecting them does not automatically produce coordinated behavior. The VLA may generate actions that diverge from the LLM's intended subtask and, upon regaining control after a correction, undo the promising state restored by the LLM. We introduce ESI (Embodied Self-Improvement), an automated flywheel that uses environmental interaction to align reasoning and action. ESI treats the modular agent as the unit of post-training, repeatedly refining the prompts that guide the LLM, the shared skill interface that expresses its intent, and the VLA parameters that realize that intent, then redeploying these components together. Our key insight is that collaboration itself can supply supervision for improving this interface. The LLM's subtask decisions provide semantic supervision for what the policy should execute, while its effective corrections and subsequent student continuations provide action-level supervision for recovery and handoff. The student also learns from its own effective execution, allowing locally useful experience to contribute even when the overall episode fails. On ten selected RoboDojo tasks, ESI achieves a mean Score of 62.03 and a mean success rate of 49.41% using an LLM-VLA agent without generating task-specific control code. On both metrics, it outperforms the published reference results of all hybrid embodied agents, including the Agent+WAM system GO-3 Nano Preview (47.27 Score and 36.60% success), as well as all compared code-based methods.

frontier.title: Objectives as Policies: Vision-Language Model Cost Programs for Contact-Rich Manipulation
frontier.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong semantic and spatial reasoning capabilities in 3D environments. Recently, connecting VLMs with model-predictive controllers (MPC) has emerged as a paradigm for combining strong semantic reasoning with physics-based planning. However, connecting these two for contact-rich robotic manipulation requires a task representation that bridges the two and captures how physical interactions can be reasoned by VLMs. In this work, we introduce Objectives as Policies (OaP), a framework that connects a pretrained VLM to a shared sampling-based MPC through an editable objective program. Each program specifies a sequence of stages for completing a task, combining running and terminal costs from a cost library with stage completion conditions. Given a natural-language task instruction and scene observation, we build a simulation-based digital twin through real-to-sim, and the VLM generates an objective program that is executed by the MPC in the simulation. The program is iteratively updated by the VLM based on MPC rollouts, before being deployed in the real world. We evaluate our framework in both simulation and the real world on four tabletop manipulation tasks, and show that it outperforms strong baselines. Additional videos and examples are available on the project website: https://zihaolu001.github.io/oap-project/

frontier.title: SceneAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Portable Game Scene Generation
frontier.abstract: Moving a scene generator to a new game engine requires more than exporting its final output: planning, construction tools, and stored experience may also depend on the original backend. We present SceneAgent, a multi-agent framework for reusing the construction process and its experience across backends. A canonical SceneContext maintains the evolving world, while backend adapters isolate coordinate conventions, asset bindings, and export. Structured handoffs let fresh Builder sessions query this persistent state without inheriting the full construction transcript. Across generations, human-approved traces are distilled into asset-ID-free Layout skills and semantic Content skills that can be retrieved and recombined. We introduce GameSceneBench, comprising 69 indoor and outdoor prompts. Under a common asset and evaluation protocol, SceneAgent obtains human tie-adjusted preference scores of 78.2-89.4% against five baselines. Ablations show that reusable skills and the multi-agent protocol primarily improve prompt alignment and scene completeness, with additional runtime. Deployment in a second engine preserves the shared construction protocol and skill library while replacing backend integration components. Together, these results support separating persistent scene state, task-local reasoning, and reusable experience for portable scene construction.

Talk to Act: A Synthetic Multi-Turn Dialogue Benchmark for Human Intent Extraction and Action Planning in Robotics
frontier.abstract: Multi-turn conversational human-robot interaction (HRI) continues to be a challenging problem in robotics, as many existing systems rely on rigid, command-driven interfaces that can be unintuitive for users. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a promising direction, given their ability to process natural language, generate structured outputs, and support tool-based reasoning, all of which are relevant for interpreting user intent in robotic settings. However, progress in this area is constrained by the limited availability of datasets and benchmarks that capture the nuances of real-world human communication, such as multi-turn dialogue, ambiguity, and context-dependent requests. In this work, we present a synthetically generated multi-turn dialogue dataset for HRI, annotated with action intents, object references, and task plans across a range of scenarios and user personas. Our primary focus is on evaluating the capability of small, open-weight language models for robotic tasks, particularly in settings where local deployment and efficiency are important. To this end, we frame intent extraction as a tool-calling problem where each predicted action corresponds to a structured function call with arguments grounded in the dialogue and benchmark models ranging from 270M to 8B parameters on their ability to perform intent extraction and action planning without task-specific fine-tuning. Our results show that these models can achieve reasonable performance on the task even at relatively small scales and without any task-specific fine-tuning. This suggests that compact, locally deployable models already provide a useful baseline for conversational robotic systems. We expect that task-specific fine-tuning and more realistic training data will enhance performance further and make such models increasingly suitable for real-world robotic applications.

Data Fragmentation as a Critical Bottleneck in Disaster Response Planning: The EVAC-AI Case Study for Flood Risk Assessment
frontier.abstract: Coastal flood risk in regions such as Hampton Roads, Virginia, is constrained not by a lack of data, but by the fragmentation of that data across agencies, formats, and update cadences. This fragmentation directly undermines risk assessment for response planning: when hazard, infrastructure, and vulnerability data remain siloed, compound risk cannot be assessed as a single picture, and response decisions are made against an incomplete view. Addressing it requires three capabilities: integrating heterogeneous sources into a consistent representation, optimizing decisions by reasoning across interconnected systems such as transportation and urban planning, and coordinating role-specific access to a shared information base. We present EVAC-AI, a knowledge-graph-grounded conversational Q\&A system designed to support all three capabilities for coastal flood evacuation planning in Virginia Beach. EVAC-AI integrates independently maintained data sources including FEMA flood zones, NOAA tide readings, evacuation routes, and Waze crowdsourced reports, into a single Neo4j knowledge graph. This graph is exposed through a natural-language query pipeline that translates user questions directly into validated, schema-refined Cypher queries, rather than retrieving subgraphs for an LLM to summarize. We argue that this design directly supports the three requirements: direct query execution preserves the structure and relationships of the graph through to the final answer, grounds multi-hop decisions in explicit and auditable graph traversals rather than generated summaries, and ensures that users in different roles receive responses backed by the same verifiable graph results. A single-page chatbot-and-map interface demonstrates the architecture in practice by returning both natural-language answers and corresponding map highlights for queries spanning flood zones, evacuation routes, and shelters.

frontier.title: From Delegates to Trustees: Aligning LLM Planners with Absent Stakeholders in Climate Decision-Making
frontier.abstract: Climate decisions, such as where to invest scarce adaptation funds, how to sequence coastal defences under sea-level rise, and how to share a carbon budget, affect constituencies that may be unable to participate in making them or systematically excluded from doing so: future generations, distant and marginalized communities, and non-human systems. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as planning assistants for such decisions, yet the dominant way of aligning them, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and its preference-based successors, aligns a model to the expressed preferences of annotators who are present, available, and demographically narrow. Borrowing a distinction from the theory of political representation, we argue that preference-based alignment implements a delegate model of representation, whereas climate planning requires a trustee model: acting in the interest of principals who cannot give feedback. We propose Trustee Alignment, a paradigm in which the alignment target is a mandate rather than a scalar reward, where a mandate is a set of constituencies, each endowed with a charter, a grounded interest model, and non-negotiable safeguards; alignment is assessed at the level of plans and their modeled consequences rather than utterances; normative uncertainty (for instance, over discount rates) is handled by an explicit parliamentary procedure rather than learned from annotators; and every plan carries a contestable ledger for human oversight. We instantiate the paradigm as an LLM-Modulo planning loop with constituency-indexed trustee critics, illustrate it on coastal adaptation pathways, and set out open problems for the planning community.

frontier.title: Meta-Cognizing Seed AI
frontier.abstract: The Common Model of Cognition (CMC) suggests a unified view of metacognition: cognition becomes metacognitive when bounded information about the agent’s own processing enters the ordinary cognitive cycle. Here we extend that commitment from human-like impasses, episodic reconstruction, and hypothetical states to a less human-like neural-symbolic seed AI that metacognizes as it evaluates and implements proposed self-modifications. Our concrete setting is the Omega architecture: an agentic cognitive cycle combining LLMs with Hyperon symbolic memory and reasoning, in which proposals are separated from the authority to act on them, and a slower GOLEM-Iter loop rewrites the cycle’s own components under protected evaluation. Current Omega instances are LLM-heavy but designed for progressively plural neural-symbolic and predictive-coding cognition. We then define metacognitive closure as an Eilenberg-Moore algebra for a resource-bounded reflection monad – in plain terms, a lawful interface through which a system writes bounded descriptions of its own processing and demonstrably consumes them – and summarize our companion mathematical paper, The Geometry and Economics of Metacognitive Self-modification, which makes the concept quantitative: hidden probes priced by description length certify how far a self-modification departs from closure, a measured repair contraction keeps accumulated drift inside an explicit tube, and the rate of trustworthy self-modification is limited by proposal entropy and evaluation capacity. Closure is thereby the migration-coherence coordinate of a larger metacognitive competence vector, not a guarantee that the self-model, evaluator, or goals are correct. We close with an evaluation ecology tied to the formal quantities and the conditions under which the program would be falsified. The result is a research program toward AGI and potentially superintelligence, tied closely to current empirical work on Omega agents.

frontier.title: SARP: A Semantic-Augmented Reinforcement Planning Framework for Mobile Robot Obstacle Avoidance and Path Optimization
frontier.abstract: Abstract This paper presents SARP, a Semantic-Augmented Reinforcement Planning framework for mobile robot navigation in complex and dynamic environments. By integrating semantic embeddings from a pre-trained language encoder with reinforcement learning, SARP constructs semantically enriched state representations that combine geometric perception and contextual knowledge. A semantic-guided policy optimization mechanism aligns efficiency, safety, and task intent, while asynchronous semantic updates decouple language encoding from the high-frequency control loop. Experiments in dynamic maze, corridor crossing, and crowded field scenarios show that SARP substantially outperforms conventional reinforcement learning baselines and achieves competitive or slightly superior navigation performance compared with representative large-language-model-aware approaches, while requiring substantially lower online semantic inference overhead. Profiling on desktop and embedded NVIDIA platforms further demonstrates a favorable performance–latency trade-off for edge deployment.

frontier.title: Toward autonomous decision support in semiconductor manufacturing: a review of planning, scheduling, dispatching, and execution control
frontier.abstract: Abstract Semiconductor manufacturing is a high-stakes cyber-physical production domain in which planning targets, scheduling feasibility, dispatching actions, process-control feedback, and human oversight must remain continuously aligned. This paper presents a structured state-of-the-art review of semiconductor smart manufacturing from the perspective of autonomous intelligent systems (AIS). The review does not treat planning, scheduling, dispatching, real-time dispatching (RTD), advanced process control (APC), manufacturing execution systems (MES), advanced planning and scheduling (APS), and enterprise resource planning (ERP) as separate production-management topics. Instead, it synthesizes them as bounded components of a human-supervised closed-loop decision architecture. The central artifact is an AIS reference model that maps fab layers to state inputs, decision-support functions, human authority, and audit or safeguard mechanisms. The review also develops a deployment-maturity matrix for classical optimization, simulation, rule-based dispatching, predictive learning, reinforcement learning, digital twins, LLM-enabled orchestration, and industrial software infrastructure. The synthesis shows that classical methods remain central because they provide interpretable constraints and executable interfaces. Learning-based and large-language-model-enabled methods can strengthen state estimation, policy adaptation, semantic mediation, and human-system interaction, but only under validated simulation or offline evaluation, bounded authority, safe fallback, access control, and auditable records. Semiconductor fabs should therefore not be described as fully autonomous systems. A more defensible AIS framing is trustworthy, human-supervised autonomous decision support: systems that sense changing fab states, evaluate alternatives, recommend or execute approved actions, and feed outcomes back into planning, scheduling, dispatching, and process-control decisions.

frontier.title: T2ST: Data-Efficient Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models via Temporal Data and Knowledge Transfer
frontier.abstract: Spatio-temporal foundation models (STFMs) require large-scale training corpora, yet synchronized observations and spatial metadata are costly to acquire and curate, limiting the availability of suitable data. By contrast, time-series data are abundant and easier to collect. Since observations at each location form a time series, this motivates a natural question: can abundant time-series data enhance STFMs when spatio-temporal observations are scarce? To bridge this gap, we propose T2ST, a data-efficient training framework that augments limited spatio-temporal observations with selected auxiliary time series and transfers knowledge from a frozen time-series foundation model. Our key insight is that temporal pattern learning can benefit from abundant external time series, while spatial dependency learning remains grounded in real spatio-temporal observations. Guided by this insight, T2ST retrieves matched sequences to reinforce sparsely observed temporal patterns and selects reliable complementary sequences to broaden temporal coverage. Temporal relation distillation aligns relationships among historical patches, while multi-scale prediction distillation transfers forecasting behavior at fine and coarse temporal resolutions, enabling knowledge transfer across heterogeneous architectures. Using only 10\% of the original spatio-temporal data, T2ST enables STFMs to achieve overall forecasting performance competitive with or superior to their full-data counterparts across six long-term and twelve short-term forecasting datasets. These results establish a new paradigm for data-efficient training of spatio-temporal foundation models. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/T2ST-65F3/.

frontier.title: Preserving Reasoning Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Adaptive Replay
frontier.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but often reduces the diversity of their reasoning behaviors. We study this phenomenon from the perspective of finite-sample learning dynamics and show that limited on-policy rollouts can progressively suppress semantically distinct but equally rewarded reasoning modes. Once a mode becomes sufficiently under-sampled, standard on-policy RLVR rarely recovers it. Motivated by this observation, we propose TAR, a Targeted Adaptive Replay framework that preserves diverse correct reasoning behaviors already present in the base policy. TAR constructs a compact memory bank of diverse base-model solutions and selectively replays them through an adaptive mechanism that activates only when stored behaviors are being suppressed during RLVR. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two Qwen2.5 model scales, TAR consistently achieves a better balance between reasoning performance and diversity preservation than existing diversity-preserving post-training methods, while substantially reducing the forgetting of correct base-model solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/wenzhilics/tar.

frontier.title: Electrically controllable superconducting memory effect in UTe2
frontier.abstract: Abstract Multiphase superconductors—materials that host two or more distinct superconductive phases—are exceptionally rare. Examples include heavy-fermion CeRh 2 As 2 alongside some uranium compounds such as UPt 3 and URhGe (refs. 1,2,3 ). In the multiphase p -wave superfluid 3 He, complex vortex dynamics can occur at the phase boundary between the A and B phases 4,5 . Here we study the p -wave superconductor candidate UTe 2 (refs. 6–8 ). On applying a magnetic field to access an intermediate regime straddling two distinct superconducting phases 9,10 , we find that direct current pulses can push the material in and out of a metastable state that has an enhanced critical current density J c . This switching is controllable by the strength and duration of the stimuli, with the system ‘remembering’ whether it is in the high or low J c state for extended periods. We interpret this phenomenology to be due to the quenching of a disordered out-of-equilibrium glassy vortex state under perturbation, which has stronger pinning forces and thus higher J c . The equilibrium vortex lattice is reattained by annealing the system with a gradual current ramp, returning it to the original state. Rather than requiring proximate magnetic or semiconducting interfaces 11–14 , this memory functionality seems to be an intrinsic property of UTe 2 rooted in the superconducting order itself. Our findings underscore the rich complexity of multiphase quantum vortex matter.

frontier.title: CRUCIBLE: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Annotation Rubric Calibration via Iterative Inter-Judge Disagreement Resolution
frontier.abstract: Annotation quality is a limiting factor in supervised learning pipelines that rely on the LLM-as-judge paradigm. This paper's central finding is that an automated convergence criterion can certify agreement that chance-corrected measurement does not support, and that the certification is an artifact of the agreement metric being optimized. Our weighted agreement statistic has a floor of 0.667 at zero unanimity, so a convergence threshold of τ = 0.80 is satisfied at 8 of 20 unanimous items: the loop halts and declares success while 60% of items still carry judge disagreement. The domain that crossed τ on this metric at 81.7% has a chance-corrected inter-judge agreement of only AC1 = 0.286. We reach this finding while building CRUCIBLE, a multi-agent system that automatically calibrates annotation rubrics through iterative, coordinator-mediated disagreement diagnosis. No human is in the loop after initialization, and no human reference labels are used during calibration. Applied to 60 YouTube transcripts across three domains, CRUCIBLE reached 96.7%, 81.7%, and 70.0% weighted inter-judge agreement, corresponding to chance-corrected AC1 of 0.929, 0.286, and -0.080. An independent human validation study covering the full corpus—20 transcripts per domain, scored by two disjoint cohorts of three annotators each—finds that judge and human chance-corrected reliability rank the three domains identically, so the judges find difficult what humans find difficult. We report as a negative result that agreement between human consensus and the system's labels carries almost no evidential weight in this design: five of six domain-round cells fail to beat a majority-class baseline that labels every item with the domain's dominant class, and the pooled rate of 75% is below the corresponding baseline. Against that baseline, a between-domain contrast we previously reported as preliminary evidence of a human-alignment dissociation does not survive. Two further interventions—porting the calibrated rubric to a frontier judge, and adding a reasoning step before the label—each move the optimized metric without moving agreement with the human reference, and a reasoning step alone moves it by +11.6 points. These results locate CRUCIBLE's value not in raising raw agreement, and not in match against human consensus, but in diagnosing whether residual disagreement is rubric-fixable, capability-bounded, or prevalence-dominated—and in the accompanying warning that a stopping rule defined on an uncorrected agreement metric will terminate before agreement has been achieved. For a safety-critical evaluation pipeline, this is the risk-relevant contribution: an operator reading 81.7% agreement as convergence is reading a number whose floor is 66.7%.

frontier.title: Agentic AI and Autonomous LLM Systems: A Scientific Literature Review
frontier.abstract: The shift of large language models (LLMs) from passive text generators to agentic systems marks a move toward autonomous intelligence. Agentic AI refers to systems that reason, plan, and execute actions in pursuit of complex goals with minimal human intervention. This paper reviews recent research on the architectural foundations, core functional modules, applications, and safety challenges of autonomous LLM systems. Current work emphasizes modular architectures in which an LLM serves as the central reasoning engine, augmented by components for perception, memory, planning, and tool interaction. Multi-agent systems have emerged as a dominant trend, enabling collaborative problem solving through structured orchestration and communication protocols. Although these systems show significant potential in software engineering, manufacturing, and cybersecurity, critical barriers remain in safety, reliability, and ethical governance. This review provides a structured overview of the state of the art and identifies key research directions for the coming years. Index Terms—agentic AI, autonomous agents, large language models, multi-agent systems, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, AI safety

frontier.title: Perspective Chapter: Governing the Autonomous Fortress – Multi-Agent AI Systems for Secure and Resilient Cloud Cybersecurity
frontier.abstract: Cybersecurity is changing from reactive, human-centered systems to highly autonomous cyber-capable agents (HACCAs) that can operate at machine speed and scale. This chapter introduces the Autonomous Fortress, an architectural framework that changes artificial intelligence from a tool that only supports analysis into a system that can make decisions, plan multiple steps, use different tools, and improve its actions through continuous reasoning. The core of the Autonomous Fortress is a large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent system (MAS). In this system, specialized agents for perception, correlation, analysis, and response work together as digital teammates to protect the environment. The framework combines different coordination methods, including a hierarchical supervisor model and swarm-based dynamic handoff, to support adaptive and context-aware decision-making. This approach goes beyond traditional machine learning systems that mainly depend on fixed rules and pattern matching. Although these secure-by-design mechanisms improve the defender’s ability to respond to cyber threats, high levels of autonomy also introduce new risks, such as prompt injection, memory poisoning, and cascading system failures. Based on national cybersecurity strategies and enterprise deployments from 2025 to 2026, this chapter presents both a technical and governance roadmap for building secure and resilient autonomous cyber defense systems in modern digital and cloud-native environments.

Vision–Language–Action Models for Robotic Manipulation: A Critical Review of Design Choices, Evidence, and Emerging Frontiers
frontier.abstract: Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models aim to unify perception, language grounding, and robot control, yet recent progress in robotic manipulation remains difficult to compare because systems differ widely in observation modalities, action interfaces, execution regimes, control horizons, and measurement boundaries. The counted analytical corpus comprises 59 unique works: 20 VLA systems in the settings-tuple audit, eight benchmark or evaluation-protocol studies, and 31 additional mechanism or context studies. Survey seeds and general background references are not included in this count. We organize the field through a five-axis design-space taxonomy: (A) perception encoding and spatial grounding; (B) action generation, control regime, and reasoning–control interface; (C) training and adaptation; (D) data provenance and embodiment; and (E) temporal horizon and stabilization. Across these axes, we synthesize five recurring reported limitation patterns—visual brittleness, action degeneration, static supervised fine-tuning limitation, embodiment gaps, and long-horizon breakdown—and consolidate them into four research gaps: reasoning–action decoupling, closed-loop control under contact, spatiotemporal grounding, and data/embodiment mismatch. To support auditable cross-paper interpretation, we introduce a comparability-first reporting schema, a taxonomy coding manual, canonical pseudocode for core VLA mechanisms, and an evidence-tier policy for calibrating claims. We further critique what LIBERO, SimplerEnv, and CALVIN can and cannot establish, showing that current benchmarks remain insufficient for strong deployment-level claims about contact-rich recovery, viewpoint robustness, embodiment transfer, long-horizon stability, and end-to-end latency.

frontier.title: Beyond Large Language Models: A Mental World Model Framework for Mental Modeling, Simulation, Evolution, and Interpretability
frontier.abstract: Understanding and simulating how subjective cognition and mental states emerge, evolve, and shape behavior is essential for advancing artificial intelligence toward deeper social cognition and general intelligence. Existing large language models (LLMs) and Theory of Mind (ToM) methods primarily infer mental states from linguistic information, lacking unified mechanisms for subjective world construction, cognitive-psychological interactions, dynamic evolution, and historical dependencies. This paper introduces the Mental World Model (MWM) and its implementation, the Multi-Branch Mental Evolution Architecture (MMEA), which explicitly constructs subjective worlds, models interactions between cognition and mental states, and simulates continuous mental evolution shaped by historical experiences. On DynToM and RecToM, MMEA achieves 96.48% and 94.00% accuracy, respectively, outperforming leading LLMs and specialized ToM methods. Additional experiments demonstrate improvements of 28.7, 39.3, and 16.6 percentage points in mental state and behavior prediction, long-sequence prediction, and implicit mental state inference, respectively. The results demonstrate that MMEA provides an interpretable framework for continuous mental modeling, enabling AI to move beyond surface-level semantic representations to infer individuals' underlying mental states from linguistic information and dynamically simulate their internal cognitive processes and evolution over time. MWM also provides a promising foundation for causal reasoning, personalized AI, sustained human-AI interaction, and future advances toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).

frontier.title: CME-SpectrumBench: Can LLMs Analyze Condensed Matter Spectral Data?
frontier.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are presently well assessed by expert-level mathematics and physics benchmarks which focus on theoretical, symbolic reasoning. However, we lack experimental benchmarks that evaluate data analysis in frontier research problems, a capability that future domain-specific foundation models must have. To this end, we present CME-SpectrumBench, an expert-designed benchmark consisting of 190 questions that measures how reliably frontier LLMs analyze research-level spectral scientific data in condensed matter experiments (CME).
